questions.q: At Stage 1 (one model, one notebook), what does this lesson recommend?
options: Build a full feature store and model registry immediately
No platform investment yet — the team doesn't know which parts of the workflow will actually repeat
Hire a dedicated platform team before training the first model
Adopt a managed platform regardless of need
questions.explain: At Stage 1, any tooling investment is premature because the team doesn't yet know which parts of the workflow will repeat. The right move is no platform yet.

questions.q: What specifically signals that a company has outgrown Stage 2 (manual repetition) and should invest in Stage 3 tooling?
options: The company hires its 100th employee
A single engineer feels mildly annoyed by a notebook once
Multiple teams independently hit the same costly, repeated manual pain
A competitor announces a new product
questions.explain: The signal is repeated, costly manual work observed across multiple teams — not a headcount milestone or a one-off annoyance.

questions.q: What is the specific failure mode of building platform tooling too early, per this lesson?
options: The tooling is built around guessed future needs that are usually wrong once real usage appears, while real pain points go unaddressed
Early tooling is always cheaper than late tooling
Early platforms automatically prevent all future production incidents
There is no real downside to building early
questions.explain: Premature platform investment gets built around guesses about future needs, which are usually wrong once real usage patterns emerge — while the system still doesn't address the pain points that actually show up later.

questions.q: At Stage 4 (hundreds of models), how does the platform team's job change compared to Stage 3?
options: It stops existing because automation has replaced it
It shifts from directly helping each team ship to building a self-service system teams use without hand-holding
It becomes purely a compliance and legal function
It merges completely with the data science team
questions.explain: At large scale, no central team can hand-hold every model through deployment, so the platform team's focus shifts to self-service systems rather than direct, per-team assistance.

questions.q: Why does the lesson say the pain at Stage 2 is specifically about copy-pasted feature logic?
options: Because copy-pasted notebooks are illegal under most data governance rules
Because fixing a bug means fixing it in every copied notebook separately, inconsistently, which is the seed of training/serving skew issues covered later
Because notebooks cannot be version controlled under any circumstances
Because copy-pasting is always faster than any platform tool
questions.explain: When feature logic is copy-pasted across notebooks, a fix has to be applied n times inconsistently — this is exactly the kind of drift that later causes training/serving skew, covered in Lesson 8.
